code: We are starting a new flagship, CRAN-grade R package in this repository: `llmmetric` — a psychometric and statistical validity framework for treating LLMs as measurement instruments in R.  Project mission: Bring formal measurement theory and valid statistical inference to LLM-coded research data (surveys, interviews, EMA diaries, clinical text): 1. Multi-facet structured coding engine (`unit × prompt × model × temperature`) with response caching, schema validation, and pluggable backends (HTTP/OpenAI-compatible APIs, local Ollama, and a deterministic mock/synthetic-rater backend for offline testing and simulations). 2. LLM Psychometrics suite: Generalizability Theory variance components, reliability & D-study projections, calibration vs. human gold standards, and Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF) / subgroup invariance tests. 3. Measurement-error-corrected downstream inference: implement Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI / PPI++) and validation-set calibration for means, linear/GLM models, and clustered/multilevel analyses so CIs and p-values stay valid when using AI-coded variables. 4. `ggplot2::autoplot` diagnostic visualizations + a Monte Carlo simulation vignette proving nominal CI coverage vs. naive LLM-score regressions.  Please start by inspecting this repo, proposing the statistical formulation, modular architecture (`ARCHITECTURE.md`), and phased implementation plan, and then we will build iteratively to full tests, vignettes, and a clean `R CMD check`.

what: Why High Overall Correlation Can Still Hide Subgroup Bias
title: Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF), Fairness, and Human Ceiling Benchmarks
text: LLM rater can achieve impressive overall correlation (r>0.85r > 0.85) human gold-standard scores still systematically - -score specific demographic, linguistic, clinical subgroups. psychometrics, failure measurement invariance known Differential Item Functioning (DIF); induced prompt wording model behavior, llmmetric terms Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF). vignette walks complete measurement-invariance fairness workflow: Benchmarking LLM agreement human inter-rater reliability ceiling via human_irr(). Detecting uniform (parallel shift) non-uniform (slope difference) DPF across multiple subgroups via dpf_test(). Pinpointing exact biased prompt template via prompt-level FDR screening prompt x group interaction test. Mitigating residual subgroup bias downstream regressions Prediction-Powered Inference (ppi_lm()) APA reporting via format_apa_table().

what: 1. Establishing the Human Inter-Rater Reliability Ceiling

what: 2. Detecting Multi-Group Uniform and Non-Uniform DPF
title: Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF), Fairness, and Human Ceiling Benchmarks
text: Now consider multi-prompt study spanning three demographic/clinical groups (group_a, group_b, group_c) three prompt templates (neutral, rubric, biased_cue), : neutral rubric largely invariant across subgroups, whereas biased_cue introduces strong uniform upward shift (+0.90) group_b modest downward shift (-0.45) group_c, overall non-uniform slope compression affects group_c. Notice two crucial methodological safeguards dpf_test(): every unit scored 3 prompts (id_col = "unit_id"), dpf_test() automatically activates unit-clustered sandwich Wald tests (clustered = TRUE), preventing pseudoreplication inflating Type-error. Per-prompt screening applies Benjamini-Hochberg FDR adjustment (omnibus_p_adj) runs global prompt x group interaction test confirming subgroup bias differs systematically across prompt wordings.   Inspecting dpf_res$prompt_interaction_test dpf_res$subgroup_summary immediately tells research team prompt dropped revised subgroups suffer conditional bias:

neutral     0.00,  0.05, -0.05,   # rubric     0.00,  0.90, -0.45    # biased_cue   ),   nrow = 3L,   ncol = 3L,   byrow = TRUE,   dimnames = list(c("neutral", "rubric", "biased_cue"), c("group_a", "group_b", "group_c")) )  des <- coding_design(   prompts = c(     neutral = "Score construct intensity objectively: {text}",     rubric = "Apply anchored rubric criteria: {text}",     biased_cue = "Evaluate emotional tone with social cues: {text}"   ),   models = "model_a",   schema = coding_schema(llm_score = schema_field("numeric")) )  be <- backend_mock(   seed = 314,   error_sd = 0.35,   prompt_sd = 0.10,   unit_prompt_sd = 0.15,   dpf_nonuniform = c(group_c = -0.35),   dpf_prompt_group = pg_bias )  coded <- code_texts(units, text_col = "text", id_col = "unit_id", design = des, backend = be)  dpf_res <- dpf_test(   coded,   score_col = "llm_score",   truth_col = "human_score",   group_col = "group",   prompt_col = "prompt",   id_col = "unit_id" ) dpf_res #>  #> ── Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF) Diagnostics #> Family: gaussian | Reference group: "group_a" | Clustered: TRUE | DPF detected: #> TRUE #> # what: 3. Mitigating Residual Bias in Downstream Regression via PPI++
title: Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF), Fairness, and Human Ceiling Benchmarks
text: Even dropping biased_cue, subtle residual calibration subgroup bias may persist rubric neutral. Suppose score larger corpus (N=700N = 700 unlabeled texts alongside n=150n = 150 human-validated texts) estimate group differences controlling covariate x:  Naive LLM severely overestimates group_b difference due DPF (~0.98 vs. true 0.40), PPI++ completely removes subgroup bias tightening confidence intervals compared using 150 human annotations alone.
code: set.seed(2028) n_tot <- 850L grp_all <- factor(sample(c("group_a", "group_b", "group_c"), n_tot, replace = TRUE)) x_all <- rnorm(n_tot) y_all <- 2.0 + 1.0 * x_all + ifelse(grp_all == "group_b", 0.4, ifelse(grp_all == "group_c", -0.3, 0)) +   rnorm(n_tot, sd = 0.85) # LLM retains uniform DPF bias (+0.65 on group_b) and slope compression llm_all <- 0.3 + 0.85 * y_all + ifelse(grp_all == "group_b", 0.65, 0) + rnorm(n_tot, sd = 0.45)  study_df <- tibble::tibble(   x = x_all,   group = grp_all,   human_score = c(y_all[1:150], rep(NA_real_, n_tot - 150L)),   llm_score = llm_all )  fit_ppi <- ppi_lm(human_score ~ x + group, data = study_df, pred_col = "llm_score") format_apa_table(fit_ppi, include_intercept = FALSE) #> **Comparison of Naive LLM, Human-Only, and PPI++ Parameter Estimates** #>  #> | Term | Estimator | Estimate | SE | 95% CI | p | Eff. Gain | #> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | #> | x | Naive LLM | 0.789 | 0.029 | [0.733, 0.845] | < .001 | -- | #> | x | Human-Only | 1.006 | 0.067 | [0.875, 1.137] | < .001 | 1.00x | #> | x | PPI++ | 0.995 | 0.047 | [0.904, 1.087] | < .001 | 2.05x | #> | groupgroup_b | Naive LLM | 1.006 | 0.072 | [0.864, 1.148] | < .001 | -- | #> | groupgroup_b | Human-Only | 0.385 | 0.153 | [0.084, 0.685] | .012 | 1.00x | #> | groupgroup_b | PPI++ | 0.394 | 0.124 | [0.150, 0.638] | .002 | 1.52x | #> | groupgroup_c | Naive LLM | -0.221 | 0.070 | [-0.358, -0.083] | .002 | -- | #> | groupgroup_c | Human-Only | -0.069 | 0.183 | [-0.427, 0.290] | .707 | 1.00x | #> | groupgroup_c | PPI++ | -0.171 | 0.122 | [-0.410, 0.068] | .162 | 2.25x | #>  #> *Note.* Labeled validation n = 150; unlabeled LLM N = 700; power-tuning lambda = 0.595. what: Why Treat LLMs as Psychometric Measurement Instruments?
title: Treating LLMs as Measurement Instruments: Getting Started with llmmetric
text: researchers use large language models (LLMs) code open-ended survey responses, therapy transcripts, daily ecological momentary assessment (EMA) diaries quantitative scores, resulting variables behave like ratings fallible human judges—except new error sources: Facet variance: scores fluctuate across prompt wordings, model families, sampling temperatures. Miscalibration & drift: LLM scores may exhibit scale compression, intercept shifts, temporal drift across API updates. Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF): prompt may systematically - -score specific demographic experimental subgroups conditional true human ratings. Invalid downstream inference: plugging biased noisy LLM scores directly regressions multilevel models produces biased slopes anti-conservative confidence intervals. llmmetric addresses four issues one cohesive workflow.

what: 1. Multi-Facet Structured Coding with Caching & Schema Validation
title: Treating LLMs as Measurement Instruments: Getting Started with llmmetric
text: production plug backend_openai() (OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint) backend_ollama() (local Ollama models). offline reproducibility, prototyping, power analysis, llmmetric provides backend_mock()—deterministic synthetic LLM rater parameterized explicit variance components, calibration bias, subgroup DPF, drift.

Specify a crossed 3 prompts x 2 models coding design design <- coding_design(   prompts = c(     direct = "Rate the speaker's emotional distress: {text}",     rubric = "Apply the clinical distress rubric to score: {text}",     cot    = "Identify emotional cues step by step, then score: {text}"   ),   models = c("model_a", "model_b"),   temperatures = 0,   schema = schema )  # title: Monte Carlo Coverage Proof: PPI / PPI++ vs. Naive LLM Regressions
text: common workflow computational social science psychology score large corpus texts (N=1,000+N = 1{,}000+) LLM fit regression multilevel model treating LLM scores Ŷ\hat{Y}_i true human measurements YiY_i. Whenever Ŷ\hat{Y}_i additive bias, scale attenuation, differential covariate error (DPF), correlated cluster errors, naive LLM regressions produce: biased point estimates, severely anti-conservative confidence intervals whose true coverage collapses far nominal 95% level—especially NN grows large (making biased CI even narrower around wrong value!). Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI, Angelopoulos et al., 2023) Power-Tuned PPI (PPI++, Angelopoulos et al., 2024) solve combining small human-validated subset (nn) large LLM-coded corpus (NN) via rectified estimating equation: LλPPI++(θ)=1n∑=1nℓθ(Xi,Yi)+λ(1N∑j=1Nℓθ(Xju,Ŷju)−1n∑=1nℓθ(Xi,Ŷ)), L_\lambda^{\text{PPI++}}(\theta) =   \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^n \ell_\theta(X_i, Y_i)   + \lambda\left(       \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \ell_\theta(X_j^u, \hat{Y}_j^u)       - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^n \ell_\theta(X_i, \hat{Y}_i)     \right), optimal plug-tuning weight λ̂*\hat{\lambda}^* minimizing asymptotic variance. vignette runs four reproducible Monte Carlo studies directly via llmmetric verify: Linear regression (ppi_lm) covariate-dependent LLM bias (DPF). Logistic regression (ppi_glm) biased LLM predicted probabilities. Multilevel clustered regression (ppi_lmer) strong intra-cluster correlation. Graceful degradation pure noise, showing PPI++ (lambda = "auto") dominates fixed PPI (lambda = 1).
code: library(llmmetric) library(ggplot2)

what: Experiment 1: Linear Regression Under Covariate-Biased LLM Scoring
title: Monte Carlo Coverage Proof: PPI / PPI++ vs. Naive LLM Regressions
text: Suppose true population regression : Yi=1.0+1.25Xi+εi,εi∼𝒩(0,1), Y_i = 1.0 + 1.25 X_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), LLM exhibits scale compression covariate-correlated bias (Differential Prompt Functioning respect XiX_i): Ŷ=0.5+0.85Yi+0.35Xi+ηi,ηi∼𝒩(0,0.452). \hat{Y}_i = 0.5 + 0.85 Y_i + 0.35 X_i + \eta_i, \qquad \eta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.45^2). draw R=200R = 200 independent datasets n=120n = 120 human-coded validation units N=1,000N = 1{,}000 unlabeled LLM-coded units, comparing Naive LLM, Human-, Standard PPI (lambda = 1), PPI++ (lambda = "auto").  Look dual win PPI++: Validity: Naive LLM coverage collapses well 20% due covariate-correlated measurement bias, whereas PPI PPI++ maintain nominal ~95% coverage. Efficiency: Compared Human-OLS (n=120n = 120), PPI++ substantially reduces RMSE shrinks confidence interval width borrowing information N=1,000N = 1{,}000 unlabeled LLM scores—without introducing bias.
code: set.seed(2026) R <- 200L n_lab <- 120L n_unlab <- 1000L true_beta <- 1.25  methods <- c("naive_llm", "human_only", "ppi", "ppi++") res_list <- vector("list", R * length(methods)) k <- 0L  for (r in seq_len(R)) {   n_tot <- n_lab + n_unlab   x <- rnorm(n_tot)   y <- 1.0 + true_beta * x + rnorm(n_tot, sd = 1.0)   f <- 0.5 + 0.85 * y + 0.35 * x + rnorm(n_tot, sd = 0.45)    df <- tibble::tibble(     x = x,     y = c(y[seq_len(n_lab)], rep(NA_real_, n_unlab)),     f = f   )    fit_pp <- ppi_lm(y ~ x, data = df, pred_col = "f", method = "ppi++")   fit_p1 <- ppi_lm(y ~ x, data = df, pred_col = "f", method = "ppi")    rows <- rbind(     fit_pp$benchmarks[fit_pp$benchmarks$term == "x", ],     fit_p1$estimates[fit_p1$estimates$term == "x", ]   )    for (m in methods) {     rr <- rows[rows$method == m, , drop = FALSE][1L, ]     k <- k + 1L     res_list[[k]] <- tibble::tibble(       rep = r,       method = m,       estimate = rr$estimate,       std_error = rr$std_error,       ci_width = rr$conf_high - rr$conf_low,       covered = rr$conf_low <= true_beta && true_beta <= rr$conf_high,       sq_err = (rr$estimate - true_beta)^2     )   } }  mc_lm <- do.call(rbind, res_list)  summary_lm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(m) {   sub <- mc_lm[mc_lm$method == m, ]   tibble::tibble(     method = m,     mean_est = mean(sub$estimate),     bias = mean(sub$estimate) - true_beta,     rmse = sqrt(mean(sub$sq_err)),     mean_se = mean(sub$std_error),     mean_ci_width = mean(sub$ci_width),     coverage_95 = mean(sub$covered)   ) })) summary_lm #> # A tibble: 4 × 7 #>   method     mean_est    bias   rmse mean_se mean_ci_width coverage_95 #>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 naive_llm      1.41 0.164   0.167   0.0287         0.112       0     #> 2 human_only     1.26 0.00855 0.0878  0.0905         0.355       0.925 #> 3 ppi            1.25 0.00371 0.0697  0.0659         0.258       0.935 #> 4 ppi++          1.26 0.00588 0.0633  0.0577         0.226       0.925 summary_lm$method_label <- factor(   summary_lm$method,   levels = c("naive_llm", "human_only", "ppi", "ppi++"),   labels = c("Naive LLM", "Human-Only", "PPI (lambda=1)", "PPI++ (auto)") )  ggplot(summary_lm, aes(x = method_label, y = coverage_95, fill = method_label)) +   geom_col(width = 0.58, alpha = 0.9) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, color = "#111827") +   geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage_95)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +   scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08), labels = function(z) paste0(round(100 * z), "%")) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#56B4E9", "#009E73")) +   labs(     title = "Empirical 95% CI Coverage Across 200 Monte Carlo Replications (OLS)",     subtitle = "Dashed line = nominal 95% coverage target; biased LLM causes Naive LLM collapse",     x = NULL,     y = "Empirical 95% CI Coverage"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(legend.position = "none")

what: Experiment 2: Logistic Regression (ppi_glm) Under Biased LLM Probabilities
title: Monte Carlo Coverage Proof: PPI / PPI++ vs. Naive LLM Regressions
text: Next test binary classification outcomes Yi∼Bernoulli(expit(−0.2+1.0Xi))Y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\text{expit}(-0.2 + 1.0 X_i)) LLM outputs biased predicted probabilities (n=180n = 180 human labels, N=1,000N = 1{,}000 unlabeled texts, R=120R = 120 replications).
code: set.seed(2027) R_glm <- 120L true_b_glm <- 1.0  glm_rows <- lapply(seq_len(R_glm), function(r) {   n_tot <- 180L + 1000L   x <- rnorm(n_tot)   p_true <- plogis(-0.2 + true_b_glm * x)   y <- rbinom(n_tot, 1L, p_true)   # Miscalibrated / attenuated LLM probability score   f <- plogis(0.6 + 0.55 * x + 0.7 * (y - p_true))   df <- tibble::tibble(     x = x,     y = c(y[1:180], rep(NA_real_, 1000L)),     f = f   )   fit <- ppi_glm(y ~ x, data = df, pred_col = "f", family = binomial())   b <- fit$benchmarks[fit$benchmarks$term == "x", ]   tibble::tibble(     method = b$method,     estimate = b$estimate,     ci_width = b$conf_high - b$conf_low,     covered = b$conf_low <= true_b_glm & true_b_glm <= b$conf_high   ) })  mc_glm <- do.call(rbind, glm_rows) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("naive_llm", "human_only", "ppi++"), function(m) {   sub <- mc_glm[mc_glm$method == m, ]   tibble::tibble(     method = m,     mean_est = mean(sub$estimate),     bias = mean(sub$estimate) - true_b_glm,     mean_ci_width = mean(sub$ci_width),     coverage_95 = mean(sub$covered)   ) })) #> # A tibble: 3 × 5 #>   method     mean_est    bias mean_ci_width coverage_95 #>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl> #> 1 naive_llm     0.542 -0.458         0.0329       0     #> 2 human_only    1.03   0.0289        0.788        0.942 #> 3 ppi++         1.03   0.0254        0.756        0.925

text: EMA diaries, therapy sessions, classroom studies, texts nested within clusters (G=80G = 80 clusters, m=5m = 5 texts per cluster, cluster random intercept SD = 0.8, residual SD = 0.7, giving ICC≈0.57\text{ICC} \approx 0.57). validate 30 clusters human raters leaving 50 clusters LLM-(disjoint validation) verify nominal coverage ppi_lmer():

what: Beyond Simple Random Validation and Linear Calibration
title: Stratified Validation Sampling, IPW-PPI, Cross-Fitted Calibration, and Custom Backends
text: Standard Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI / PPI++) assumes human-validated subset drawn simple random sampling (SRS) uses linear gradient rectifiers raw LLM predictions. real applied studies, researchers routinely encounter three additional challenges: Unequal-probability validation sampling (select_validation_sample() + IPW-PPI): minority subgroup represents 15% corpus—extreme scores matter —researchers oversample rare strata maximize Differential Prompt Functioning (DPF) power Neyman precision. Passing exact inclusion probabilities πi\pi_i Horvitz-Thompson weights wi=1/πiw_i = 1/\pi_i ppi_mean() ppi_lm() activates exact Active / IPW-PPI++ estimation (Zrnic & Candès, 2024). Non-linear LLM score distortion (ppi_calibrated()): LLM ratings frequently suffer floor/ceiling compression, S-curve saturation, covariate-dependent non-linear distortion. ppi_calibrated() learns KK-fold cross-fitted natural spline, polynomial, logistic, custom calibrator strictly --fold applying PPI++, preserving exact unbiasedness slashing standard errors. Offline custom scoring pipelines (backend_custom()): Many research teams run local open-weights models, institutional endpoints, offline packages (airgapllm) rather hosted APIs. backend_custom() wraps R callable code_texts() zero added dependencies.

text: Consider corpus M=1,500M = 1{,}500 open-ended responses underrepresented subgroup (group = "minority", 15% corpus) higher true distress mean stronger predictor slope, LLM exhibits systematic downward bias slope attenuation: ensure adequate statistical power minority-group DPF auditing, draw n=160n = 160 human validation texts using equal allocation across two subgroups (80 majority + 80 minority)—oversampling minority stratum nearly 6×6\times: Notice Horvitz-Thompson weights wi=1/πiw_i = 1 / \pi_i sum exactly corpus size M=1,500M = 1{,}500: minimizing overall variance primary goal (rather balanced subgroup DPF power), strategy = "neyman" allocates validation budget proportionally Nh⋅SDhN_h \cdot \mathrm{SD}_h using observed LLM scores:
code: set.seed(2026) M <- 1500 group <- factor(   c(rep("majority", 1275), rep("minority", 225)),   levels = c("majority", "minority") ) x <- rnorm(M) is_min <- as.numeric(group == "minority")  # True outcome: mean differs sharply across groups and slope depends on x y_true <- 2.0 + 1.2 * x + 1.8 * is_min + rnorm(M, sd = 0.9)  # Biased, attenuated LLM proxy with subgroup DPF y_llm <- 0.9 + 0.65 * y_true - 0.8 * is_min + 0.35 * x + rnorm(M, sd = 0.5)  corpus <- tibble::tibble(   unit_id = sprintf("u%04d", seq_len(M)),   group = group,   x = x,   llm_score = y_llm,   true_y = y_true ) vs_equal <- select_validation_sample(   corpus,   n = 160,   strategy = "stratified",   strata_col = "group",   allocation = "equal",   seed = 101 ) vs_equal #>  #> ── Validation Sample Plan (stratified / equal) #> Selected 160 of 1500 units (10.7%) | Weight range: [2.81, 15.94] #> # A tibble: 2 × 6 #>   stratum  n_pop n_selected inclusion_prob weight stratum_sd #>   <chr>    <int>      <int>          <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl> #> 1 majority  1275         80         0.0627  15.9          NA #> 2 minority   225         80         0.356    2.81         NA sum(vs_equal$weights[vs_equal$selected]) #> [1] 1500 vs_neyman <- select_validation_sample(   corpus,   n = 160,   strategy = "neyman",   strata_col = "group",   score_col = "llm_score",   seed = 101 ) vs_neyman$stratum_summary #> # A tibble: 2 × 6 #>   stratum  n_pop n_selected inclusion_prob weight stratum_sd #>   <chr>    <int>      <int>          <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl> #> 1 majority  1275        135          0.106   9.44       1.33 #> 2 minority   225         25          0.111   9          1.36

title: Stratified Validation Sampling, IPW-PPI, Cross-Fitted Calibration, and Custom Backends
text: Now suppose human annotators code n=160n = 160 units selected vs_equal, leaving remaining N=1,340N = 1{,}340 units unlabeled (NA). minority rows heavily oversampled validation set, unweighted mean regression labeled sample severely overstates population mean! Supplying inclusion_prob = "inclusion_prob" (weights = "sampling_weight") activates exact Horvitz-Thompson Active IPW-PPI++: Horvitz-Thompson weighting applies seamlessly linear regression via ppi_lm():  IPW-PPI++ accurately recovers population intercept, predictor slope, subgroup difference shrinking confidence intervals substantially relative IPW Human-estimation—avoiding dramatic bias Naive LLM regression.

A tibble: 4 × 3 #>   estimator                 estimate std_error #>   <chr>                        <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 True Population Mean          2.25   NA      #> 2 Naive LLM                     2.24    0.0345 #> 3 Unweighted PPI++ (Biased)     2.79    0.0807 #> 4 IPW-PPI++ (Valid)             2.34    0.0704 fit_lm_ipw <- ppi_lm(   human_score ~ x + group,   data = study_df,   pred_col = "llm_score",   inclusion_prob = "inclusion_prob" ) fit_lm_ipw #>  #> ── Prediction-Powered Inference (ipw_ppi++) #> Labeled n = 160 | Unlabeled N = 1340 | lambda = 0.554 | CI = 95% #> IPW weighted active inference | Kish effective labeled n = 107.4 #> # A tibble: 3 × 7 #>   term          estimate std_error conf_low conf_high p_value var_gain #>   <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> #> 1 (Intercept)       2.11    0.0672     1.98      2.25 <0.0001     1.95 #> 2 x                 1.31    0.0609     1.20      1.43 <0.0001     1.39 #> 3 groupminority     1.64    0.135      1.38      1.90 <0.0001     1.26 format_apa_table(fit_lm_ipw) #> **Comparison of Naive LLM, Human-Only, and IPW_PPI++ Parameter Estimates** #>  #> | Term | Estimator | Estimate | SE | 95% CI | p | Eff. Eff. Gain denotes variance reduction (effective sample-size multiplier) relative to Human-Only. autoplot(   fit_lm_ipw,   true_values = c("(Intercept)" = 2.0, x = 1.2, groupminority = 1.8) )

title: Stratified Validation Sampling, IPW-PPI, Cross-Fitted Calibration, and Custom Backends
text: Even simple random validation sampling, raw LLM scores often non-linearly distorted (example, compressed narrow S-curve 0 5 covariate-dependent shift). Standard linear PPI++ remains unbiased, variance reduction limited linear correlation YY Ŷ\hat{Y}. ppi_calibrated() learns non-linear mapping m̂(Ŷ,X)≈Y\hat{m}(\hat{Y}, X) \approx Y via strict KK-fold cross-fitting labeled subset (splines::ns(), polynomial, logistic, user-supplied learner) every labeled prediction strictly --fold every unlabeled prediction uses exact fold-weighted average KK models: Notice --fold spline calibration dramatically boosts human-LLM correlation (r_raw r_calibrated_oof) cuts prediction RMSE, translating directly tighter, provably valid confidence intervals compared Human-uncalibrated PPI++:  Researchers can also supply completely custom calibration learner via calibrator = function(train_df, new_df, truth_col, pred_col, rhs_vars) { ... } (instance, wrapping random forest, GAM, gradient-boosted tree another package).
code: set.seed(2027) M_nl <- 1200 n_lab <- 160 x_nl <- rnorm(M_nl) g_nl <- factor(sample(c("control", "treatment"), M_nl, replace = TRUE)) y_nl <- 1.0 + 1.3 * x_nl + 0.7 * (g_nl == "treatment") + rnorm(M_nl, sd = 0.75)  # Severe S-curve ceiling/floor compression + covariate shift llm_nl <- 5 * stats::plogis(1.5 * (y_nl - 1.2) + 0.6 * x_nl) + rnorm(M_nl, sd = 0.18)  df_nl <- tibble::tibble(   x = x_nl,   group = g_nl,   human_y = c(y_nl[seq_len(n_lab)], rep(NA_real_, M_nl - n_lab)),   llm_y = llm_nl )  fit_cal <- ppi_calibrated(   human_y ~ x + group,   data = df_nl,   pred_col = "llm_y",   calibrator = "spline",   df = 4L,   folds = 5L,   seed = 2027 ) fit_cal #>  #> ── Prediction-Powered Inference (ppi++_calibrated) #> Labeled n = 160 | Unlabeled N = 1040 | lambda = 0.772 | CI = 95% #> Cross-fitted calibration (spline, 5-fold, df=4): r 0.938 -> 0.963 | RMSE 1.491 #> -> 0.423 #> # A tibble: 3 × 7 #>   term           estimate std_error conf_low conf_high p_value var_gain #>   <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> #> 1 (Intercept)       0.941    0.0558    0.831     1.05  <0.0001     1.86 #> 2 x                 1.29     0.0486    1.20      1.39  <0.0001     1    #> 3 grouptreatment    0.840    0.0743    0.695     0.986 <0.0001     2.02 format_apa_table(fit_cal, include_intercept = FALSE) #> **Comparison of Naive LLM, Human-Only, and PPI++_CALIBRATED Parameter Estimates** #>  #> | Term | Estimator | Estimate | SE | 95% CI | p | Eff. Gain | #> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | #> | x | Naive LLM | 1.493 | 0.031 | [1.432, 1.554] | < .001 | -- | #> | x | Human-Only | 1.313 | 0.049 | [1.218, 1.408] | < .001 | 1.00x | #> | x | PPI++ (Uncal.) | 1.309 | 0.048 | [1.214, 1.403] | < .001 | -- | #> | x | PPI++ (Calibrated) | 1.292 | 0.049 | [1.197, 1.387] | < .001 | 1.00x | #> | grouptreatment | Naive LLM | 0.655 | 0.054 | [0.549, 0.761] | < .001 | -- | #> | grouptreatment | Human-Only | 0.949 | 0.106 | [0.741, 1.156] | < .001 | 1.00x | #> | grouptreatment | PPI++ (Uncal.) | 0.932 | 0.097 | [0.741, 1.122] | < .001 | -- | #> | grouptreatment | PPI++ (Calibrated) | 0.840 | 0.074 | [0.695, 0.986] | < .001 | 2.02x | #>  #> *Note.* Labeled validation n = 160; unlabeled LLM N = 1040; power-tuning lambda = 0.772. Eff. Gain denotes variance reduction (effective sample-size multiplier) relative to Human-Only. autoplot(fit_cal, true_values = c(x = 1.3, grouptreatment = 0.7))

what: 4. Integrating Local & Offline Models via backend_custom()
title: Stratified Validation Sampling, IPW-PPI, Cross-Fitted Calibration, and Custom Backends
text: workflow uses local open-weights LLM, institutional Python/C++ runner, air-gapped R package (airgapllm), backend_custom() adapts R function fn(request) directly code_texts()—giving full JSON schema validation, retry handling, content-addressed disk caching, resumable checkpointing, direct entry g_study(), dpf_test(), ppi_lm() zero added dependencies: resulting llm_coded_data object flows directly g_study(), d_study(), calibration_metrics(), dpf_test(), ppi_lm().
code: # Wrap any local scorer into an llmmetric backend local_scorer <- backend_custom(   fn = function(req) {     # Inspect req$text, req$prompt_id, req$model, req$temperature, req$schema     base_val <- 2.5 + 0.08 * nchar(req$text)     prompt_shift <- if (identical(req$prompt_id, "rubric_v2")) 0.35 else 0.0     list(score = min(max(round(base_val + prompt_shift, 2), 1), 7))   },   name = "local_airgap_scorer",   version = "1.0" ) local_scorer #>  #> ── LLM Backend (custom) #> ID: custom_63e41e92ca63 #> Name: local_airgap_scorer | Version: 1.0  sample_texts <- tibble::tibble(   unit_id = paste0("doc_", 1:6),   text = c(     "Calm morning walk.",     "Feeling tense before the clinic review.",     "Overwhelmed by back-to-back deadlines and poor sleep.",     "Peaceful afternoon reading outside.",     "Anxious about upcoming travel and family obligations.",     "Steady focus throughout the workday."   ) )  design <- coding_design(   prompts = c(     rubric_v1 = "Rate distress 1-7: {text}",     rubric_v2 = "Score emotional strain 1-7: {text}"   ),   models = "local-8b" )  coded <- code_texts(   data = sample_texts,   text_col = "text",   id_col = "unit_id",   design = design,   backend = local_scorer,   cache = coding_cache("memory") ) coded$data[, c("unit_id", "prompt", "model", "score", "cache_hit")] #> NULL

title: Psychometric Validation and Inference for LLM-Coded Data
text: Psychometric reliability, measurement invariance, error-corrected statistical inference LLM-coded research data R. Researchers across psychology, education, sociology, management, health sciences increasingly use large language models (LLMs) code open-ended survey responses, therapy transcripts, interviews, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) diaries quantitative variables. Treating LLM outputs error-free gold-standard measurements ignores prompt sensitivity, model drift, subgroup bias, measurement error—invalidating standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values downstream analyses. llmmetric bridges modern AI annotation pipelines formal psychometric & statistical theory treating LLMs explicitly fallible measurement instruments.
